newsitem.title: BARBADOS: U.S. to support extension of peace force in Haiti.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to support extension of peace force in Haiti.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton told Haiti's leader on Saturday that he supports a Haitian request to extend the stay of an international peacekeeping force there from July until November, U.S. officials said.
Clinton told Haitian President Rene Preval at a summit of Caribbean leaders that the United States was consulting with other countries to try to arrange the extension, they said.

"The president is ... very sympathetic to the request, wants to work with (Preval) and with the (U.N.) Security Council and potential troop contributors to figure out how that would come to life," Deputy National Security Adviser James Steinberg said.

A U.N. peacekeeping force first went to Haiti in March 1995 to take over from a U.S.-led force which had intervened six months earlier in the Caribbean island to oust a military junta and restore elected President Jean-Bertrand Aristide.
Preval succeeded Aristide after December 1995 elections.

Amid continuing insecurity in Haiti, the U.N. force's mandate has already been extended several times, although its numbers have declined from an original 6,000 to around 1,300 now -- about 700 Canadians and the rest Pakistanis.
U.N. officials have said they hope the current extension -- until July 30 -- will be the last, but Canada has already said it plans to keep troops there until the end of the year.

Without referring directly to the troop issue, Clinton told reporters before meeting Preval: "We are determined to do whatever we can to see that democracy survives and thrives. President Preval is as well. We are going to work together."
James Dobbins, National Security Council director for inter-American affairs, said it was not certain the peacekeepers' stay would be extended.
But, he told reporters, "the extensions have occurred previously and this is not an unusual time to be discussing with other countries whether to extend and on what basis."
The United States has approximately 450 soldiers in Haiti, but they are mainly engineering and medical troops with no combat role and do not form part of the U.N. force.
Dobbins told reporters that Clinton promised Preval $10 million in aid available this year for agricultural credits to small farmers.
He said it would be of a type known as PL-480 whereby agricultural produce is shipped in and sold for local currency which can be used for specified purposes.

Steinberg said Preval told other Caribbean leaders at a lunch earlier that Haiti planned to apply for membership of CARICOM, the 14-nation Caribbean grouping in which it currently holds observer status.
